lines.text: Strike a match in a dark room. For a moment it is the brightest thing there is… and in a few seconds, it burns out.
Light a candle from it, and you get a few hours. A little stick of wax, slowly burning down to a puddle.
Now look out of the window. The Sun is coming up, just as it did yesterday, and every day for billions of years.
Speed up time. Candle after candle burns down on the sill, a whole forest of wax… and the Sun hasn’t even flickered.
So what is it burning? What fuel could possibly last that long, in a place where nobody can ever go?
To find out, we needed a lump of coal, a shrinking star, a missing scrap of weight… and ghosts at the bottom of a gold mine.
The trouble is, the Sun is a hundred and fifty million kilometres away. Nobody can fetch a piece of it to test.
And its heart is buried under seven hundred thousand kilometres of glowing gas. You could never look inside it, not even once.
For centuries people watched the Sun through smoked glass and the first telescopes. They saw dark spots drift across it… but never what made it shine.
So the scientists did the only thing they could. They took every fuel they knew, and asked: how long would it last?
Start with the obvious answer: fire. Imagine the whole Sun as one gigantic lump of coal.
Coal burns hot and bright. A heap the size of the Sun would make a fire beyond anything on Earth.
But fire eats its fuel. Run the clock forward, and a coal Sun burns right through itself in just a few thousand years.
A few thousand years is nothing. Human history alone is about that long, and the Earth was clearly far, far older.
Coal could not do it. No fire could. Scientists needed a fuel that could keep the Sun going far longer. But what could it possibly be?
In the 1850s, Hermann von Helmholtz in Germany, and William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, in Scotland, had a cleverer idea.
Squeeze something, and it warms up. Pump a bicycle tyre hard, and feel how hot the pump gets.
Now let gravity do the squeezing. The Sun’s own weight pulls it inward, and as it slowly shrinks, it glows hot.
Wrap a tape measure round its middle, and year after year the tape pulls a little tighter. Far too little to notice from Earth.
Kelvin did the sums. Squeezing could keep the Sun shining for about twenty million years: thousands of times longer than coal.
It sounded like a triumph. But out in the quarries, geologists were reading a very different calendar.
Layer on layer of rock, each one laid down grain by grain. Their slow stacking spoke of hundreds of millions of years.
And Charles Darwin needed even more. Living things change so slowly that twenty million years was nowhere near enough.
Physics said the Sun was young. Rocks and life said the Earth was old. They could not both be right.
The answer came from somewhere nobody expected. In 1920, the scientist Francis Aston weighed atoms more exactly than anyone before.
A helium atom is made of the same stuff as four hydrogen atoms. So it ought to weigh exactly the same as four.
It doesn’t. Helium is lighter, by about one part in a hundred and twenty. A sliver of weight has simply gone missing.
Where did it go? Albert Einstein had already given the answer. A little mass can turn into a huge amount of energy.
The c is the speed of light, multiplied by itself: a gigantic number. So a crumb of lost weight becomes a flood of light.
That August, in Cardiff, the astronomer Arthur Eddington put it all together. The Sun, he said, must be turning hydrogen into helium.
And the old shrinking-Sun idea? Eddington called it an “unburied corpse”. It was time to put it in the ground.
But how, exactly? Deep in the middle of the Sun it is crushed and fierce, millions of degrees hot.
Shrink down to the size of an atom’s heart. Bare hydrogen cores, called protons, rush about, and shove each other away.
Like two magnets held the wrong way round, they won’t touch. But in that heat, now and then, two crash close enough to stick.
In 1938 and 1939, Hans Bethe worked out each step: how four hydrogens, one by one, become a single helium. The lost weight leaves as sunlight.
It was a beautiful idea. But could anyone prove it? You can’t push a thermometer into the middle of the Sun.
Then came a strange clue. Each time the Sun makes helium, it also spits out a tiny particle, called a neutrino.
Neutrinos are like ghosts. They fly straight out of the Sun, across space, and right through the whole Earth, as if it were glass.
Billions of them pass through your thumbnail every second, day and night. You have never felt a single one.
Catch a few, and you could count what the Sun’s heart is doing right now. A chemist named Ray Davis decided to try.
In the 1960s, he went down the Homestake gold mine in South Dakota. How deep? Almost one and a half kilometres underground.
The rock above blocks out everything else; only the ghosts get through. He filled a tank as big as a house with cleaning fluid.
Once in a long while, a neutrino strikes an atom in the fluid and turns it into a different atom. It’s like one grain of sand turning to gold.
Davis fished out those few changed atoms and counted them, week after week, year after year.
Theory said how many he should catch. But his count came to only about a third of it.
Two thirds of the Sun’s ghosts were missing. Was the experiment wrong? Or was the Sun not burning the way everyone thought?
Some physicists blamed Davis’s tank. Others blamed the theory of the Sun. Davis just kept counting, and his number would not budge.
For thirty years nobody could say. The prediction hung on the wall while posters changed, and hair turned grey.
The answer came from another mine, in Canada. Deep underground sat a giant ball of heavy water, a rare, weightier kind of water. Thousands of electric eyes watched it.
It could catch neutrinos of every kind. And it turns out there are three kinds, like three different flavours.
And on the long flight from the Sun, a neutrino can change from one kind into another.
Davis’s tank could only see one kind. The missing two thirds had never been missing at all. They had changed their coats.
In 2001 and 2002, Sudbury counted all three kinds together. Would the total match the prediction? It did. The Sun really is a nuclear furnace.
Ray Davis won a Nobel Prize in 2002. The neutrino hunters behind the final answer won one in 2015.
So here is what the Sun really is. Every second, it turns about four million tonnes of itself into light.
It has been doing that for four and a half billion years, and it has billions of years still to go.
That light grows our wheat and our rice. It runs through a solar panel. It warms your face on a cold morning.
Every bit of it began as a sliver of lost weight, deep in the Sun’s crushing heart, where hydrogen becomes helium.
We found all this out without ever going there. Just a lump of coal, a balance, a typewriter, and a tank of cleaning fluid deep under the ground.
Go back to the window. The candle is long gone, burnt down to a puddle of wax. And the Sun is still rising.
